newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Carmakers battle over stagnant Euro market.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Carmakers battle over stagnant Euro market.

text.p: The world's carmarkers unveiled dozens of eye-catching models at the Paris car show on Tuesday, hoping to gain an edge in a cut-throat but stagnant European market.

Manufacturers packed every segment of the market with new entries, ranging from Ford Motor Co 's Ka minicar to Porsche's sporty new Boxster, to inspire reluctant customers when the show opens to the public on Thursday.
News that new car sales in France surged by a freak 86 percent in September did little to dispel the car industry's gloomy outlook for the remainder of the year and for 1997.

Experts attributed the September sales rally to last-minute purchases befored a new-cars-for-old rebate scheme expired on Monday. They expect French car sales to plunge in coming months, dragging down the European market.
"For 1997, forecasts are still very pessimistic with no expected growth," Jacques Calvet, chairman of French carmaker PSA Peugeot Citroen, told a news conference.

He said consumers were feeling the burden of fiscal belt-tightening throughout Europe as governments struggle to meet the budget criteria set in the Maastricht Treaty to create a single European currency.
"While these policies might in the end encourage economic recovery in Europe, in the very short term they are sure to cause stagnation," Calvet said.
Consulting firm DRI/McGraw Hill expects western European car sales to grow by just 0.6 percent in 1997 after an estimated rise this year of 5.8 percent to 12.7 million.

The British and Italian markets are expected to grow by more than two percent and the German market is expected to grow 1.3 percent, but the French market is expected to shrink by nearly six percent in 1997, said DRI car analyst Arthur Maher.
German manufacturers of luxury cars, BMW and Mercedes-Benz complained that company car taxes were crimping demand.
"The Italian market isn't very good right now," Fiat SpA managing director Roberto Testore told reporters.
He said third-quarter sales were not encouraging, but the group expected to boost sales in the rest of Europe by 40 percent this year, helped by a renewed product line.
Fiat's success in Europe is also due to the Italian lira's relative weakness against the German mark and the French franc although the Italian currency has rebounded from its lows.

In a market distorted by incentive schemes, currency fluctuations, import quotas on Japanese cars and a fierce price war, carmakers are trying to shift the spotlight back onto products designed for evolving tastes and demographics.
But they are bolstering their launches with aggressive marketing campaigns in a sign that suggests the price rivalry in Europe is not about to subside.

Renault announced last week that it would lower car prices through outright reductions or by adding equipment at no extra charge. "To sell cars you need two things -- cars that people feel like buying, and prices they can afford," Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer said in an interview with the Figaro newspaper.
Volvo Cars will launch a marketing offensive in the fourth quarter to recapture lost market share in Europe, and Fiat will offer rebates in France for buyers turning in old clunkers.
Officials at Volkswagen, which has increased its leadership position in the European market by keeping down prices, said the company will continue to restrain price increases.
The Peugeot group, ranked third among Europe's Big Six carmakers, also said it would not match its rivals' price cuts to preserve its profit margins.

But competition is expected to widen as carmakers venture into new niches to broaden their model line-ups and establish a presence in promising segments such as minicars and multi-purpose vehicles expected to outpace the overall market.
Mercedes-Benz made its debut in the minicar segment with the introduction at the show of a luxury A class model.
